newsitem.title: USA: US Treasury 3-yr note sale poor, but mart hangs in.
newsitem.headline: US Treasury 3-yr note sale poor, but mart hangs in.

text.p: If the three-year note auction was supposed to be the smoothest of the three legs of the Treasury's quarterly refunding, the rest of the week will be treacherous for the U.S. Treasuries.
Investors balked at the sale of $18.5 billion in three-year notes, which came in mostly as expected at an average yield of 5.879 percent.
"The auction did not go well," said a senior trader at a primary dealership. "But the market's hanging in. I thought for sure we'd crack back.

Going into the session, traders were optimistic about the auction's success. Some said it was a piece of cake, in that it would be easier to take down than the 10-year and 30-year issues Wednesday and Thursday, respectively.
But the when-issued three-year note of 5.92 percent from Monday became 5.87 percent Tuesday, after mostly foreign accounts led a morning rally.
"We had to build in a concession and we did," said a head trader at a U.S. bank. "The fact we got beyond 5.88 1/2 (percent) is pretty impressive."

Unimpressive, though, were non-competitive bids, which came in at $564 million -- below even the most optimistic projections. Meanwhile, the bid to cover ratio was 2.28, less than the 2.3 or higher expected by the market and below the average 2.5 seen in the past 24 three-year note auctions.
Traders said the auction would have been a success if the market didn't rally so much this morning.
"The market went too far too fast," the head trader said. "The market has had a pause and we're still in pretty good shape...Now, we're waiting to see what the election will bring us."
Since the auction results were announced, the when-issued three-year note has traded at a slight profit, edging back down to 5.88 percent.

Waldo Best, an economist at BZW Securities, disagreed that the auction was awful. "There was nothing wrong with it; it was as expected," he said. "Anyone selling on these results are really fishing for an exucse to sell."
Now that the three-year note is gone, the market is now setting up for the 10-year note sale Wednesday. But Best said current levels -- 6.29 percent -- are too expensive.
